summary: Defines behavioral characteristics of Internet firewalls and requirements for their interoperability. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A firewall can block traffic a site considers inappropriate, but it should not accidentally break legitimate uses of network protocols. RFC 2979 describes this expectation and gives examples.

questions: how should an internet firewall behave
what is a firewall transparency rule
what is the firewall transparency rule
subtitle: Behavioral requirements intended to keep firewalls from breaking legitimate network traffic.

tldr.problem: Unspecified firewall behavior can cause standards-compliant applications to fail for reasons that are difficult to diagnose.
tldr.mechanism: The memo states a transparency rule: a firewall must not cause unintended failures for legitimate, standards-compliant use that would work without it. It applies the rule to examples involving ICMP and SMTP extensions.
tldr.outcome: Sites may still block access they consider illegitimate, but firewalls should handle permitted traffic without gratuitous failures. RFC 2979 is Informational.

today: RFC 2979 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Firewall Does
sections.content:
A firewall screens network traffic and may block traffic it considers inappropriate or dangerous. It can act as a protocol endpoint and relay, as a packet filter, or use both approaches.

Firewall functions are separate from Network Address Translation (NAT), though one device can provide both. RFC 2979 addresses firewall behavior because inconsistent or underspecified behavior can cause practical interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall decides which network traffic can pass. It may inspect packets directly or take part in a protocol as a server or relay.

sections.title: The Transparency Rule
sections.content:
The memo says that adding a firewall or related tunneling and access-negotiation facilities MUST NOT cause unintended failures of legitimate, standards-compliant use that would work without the firewall. If such failures occur, the firewall and its associated software must address them.

The rule does not require a site to allow every connection. A site may block access it considers illegitimate. A firewall may also offer authentication or authorization facilities, but it MUST allow configurations that do not require those facilities for traversal.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall may block access a site rejects. But when it permits a legitimate protocol use, it should not break that use by mishandling the traffic.

sections.title: ICMP and SMTP Examples
sections.content:
Path MTU Discovery depends on ICMP Fragmentation Needed errors. If a packet-filtering firewall allows outgoing packets with the Don't Fragment bit set, it MUST allow the corresponding incoming errors to reach the inside host.

For SMTP extension negotiation, a firewall acting as an endpoint cannot simply allow the EHLO command. It must also inspect the server's response and pass through only extensions it understands, or the client and server may agree to use an extension that the firewall cannot handle.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting an SMTP request through is not enough if the firewall mishandles the answer. Likewise, a firewall that allows a large packet must not block the ICMP message needed to adjust its size.

sections.title: Advice for Application Designers
sections.content:
Application protocols SHOULD make firewall operation easier when this does not harm the application in other ways. Specifications MAY state what firewalls need to do to handle a protocol correctly.

The memo discourages wrapping a new protocol in HTTP and using port 80 just because it is likely to be open. It recommends a secure subset, an appropriate traversal mechanism where one exists, and a separate registered port for a new protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Design applications so firewalls can handle them clearly. Do not disguise a new protocol as HTTP just to get through a firewall.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
The memo recognizes that security measures can sometimes cause interoperability failures. It rejects gratuitous failures, arguing that users may otherwise disable or work around firewalls in ways that weaken security.

The transparency rule does not set a site's security policy; it concerns how the firewall handles permitted, legitimate traffic. The memo's aim is to make firewall behavior more consistent with accepted IP protocol practices.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall that breaks useful traffic may lead people to disable it or bypass it. Clear behavior can support both interoperability and security.
